newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila sees China's probing in Spratlys continuing.
newsitem.headline: Manila sees China's probing in Spratlys continuing.

text.p: Philippines defence chief Renato de Villa said on Wednesday he expected China to conduct "probing" activities into disputed isles in the South China Sea to assert its sovereignty.

He also said the Philippines' Mutual Defence Treaty with the United States was a factor in the Spratlys dispute, even if the pact did not explicitly state Manila could invoke U.S. aid in case of trouble in the South China Sea.

The Philippines last month protested against what it said was the incursion of Chinese armed vessels in areas claimed by Manila in the Spratly Islands, a cluster of low-lying isles and reefs believed to be potentially rich in oil.
Beijing, which says the Spratlys and all other islands in the South China Sea historically belong to China, said the ships were Bureau of Fisheries vessels engaged in scientific research.
The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philipines, Malaysia and Brunei.

"We cannot very precisely determine what China is attempting to achieve in this assertion of sovereign authoritity over these shoals (and) isles by various actions including use...of their Bureau of Fisheries vessels and their sports associations," de Villa told a Senate defence committee hearing on the incident.

"But we can surmise (that) in the promotion of their own interest, I think it can be expected that some activity every now and then surfaces, specially when sovereignty over a given area that is disputed is the issue."

China last week slammed the hoisting of a Philippine flag over a contested rock called Scarborough Shoal, also in the South China Sea, and accused Philippine naval ships of disrupting activities in the area by Chinese amateur radio groups.
De Villa said Manila's defence treaty with Washington was important in maintaining regional stability.
"Even if the treaty does not explicitly say it can be invoked with respect to the South China Sea problems, I still consider it a plus factor...on our side," he said.
American diplomats have said disputed areas are not covered by the scope of Washington's mutual defence treaty with Manila.
